metadata.file_name: 48. Pan & Cutumisu. (2022). Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students' life satisfaction in PISA 2018.pdf
metadata.title: Using machine learning to predict UK and Japanese secondary students' life satisfaction in PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data for two countries (UK and Japan) and restricted the analytic sample to students with complete enough data after preprocessing. The authors report imputing missing values using series mean and normalizing features for KNN, but they do not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation. Because the models are implemented with scikit-learn (Random Forest regression and KNN regression), the manuscript does not describe any complex survey weighting strategy, suggesting an unweighted ML analysis. Consequently, the results should be interpreted as predictive associations within the analyzed samples rather than population-representative estimates for all PISA 2018 students in each country.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is the PISA 2018 life satisfaction scale score derived from student self-reports (0–10), and the paper does not describe using PV-based achievement scaling. Instead, the analysis treats life satisfaction as a continuous response for supervised regression. Missing data handling is reported (series mean imputation), so the missing-data strategy is not a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Students were selected from PISA 2018 for the United Kingdom (GBR) and Japan (JPN). The dependent variable was life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA) from the PISA 2018 student questionnaire, and the model used 26 individual-level questionnaire variables (Table 2) as predictors. Missing values were imputed using series mean (missingness <10% overall), and for KNN the features were normalized; both RF and KNN were trained and tested on the same preprocessed dataset. No additional grade/school-type restrictions are reported beyond using the PISA 2018 student sample for these two countries.

top_predictors: ICT resources at home and school (ICTRES)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (nested CV, 5 outer folds): Test R² ≈ 0.187 (mean), RMSE ≈ 0.451 (mean). KNN regression (nested CV, 5 outer folds): Test R² ≈ 0.103 (mean), RMSE ≈ 0.474 (mean).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 UK the study leveraged meaning in life, motivation to master tasks, student competition, ICT resources, and exposure to bullying to predict students' life satisfaction, finding that Random Forest outperformed KNN on both validation and test performance (higher R² and lower RMSE). This indicates that combining multiple psychosocial and school-experience variables in non-linear models may better identify students at risk of lower life satisfaction, though the study reports predictive associations rather than causal effects and does not apply survey weights.

top_predictors: ICT resources at home and school (ICTRES)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression (nested CV, 5 outer folds): Test R² ≈ 0.138 (mean), RMSE ≈ 0.464 (mean). KNN regression (nested CV, 5 outer folds): Test R² ≈ 0.055 (mean), RMSE ≈ 0.486 (mean).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Japan the study leveraged meaning in life, self-efficacy, student competition, teacher support, and ICT resources to predict students' life satisfaction, finding that Random Forest again outperformed KNN (substantially higher R² and lower RMSE). This indicates that school climate and individual psychological resources jointly relate to life satisfaction in Japan, but the cross-sectional, questionnaire-based design and unweighted ML approach limit population generalization and causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2018 student questionnaire and well-being questionnaire data for two countries (UK: 13,818; Japan: 6,109) and predicted students’ life satisfaction (ST016Q01NA, 0–10) using supervised ML regression. Two models were compared under nested cross-validation with five outer folds and five inner folds for hyperparameter tuning: Random Forest and k-nearest neighbours (KNN). Random Forest achieved higher predictive performance than KNN in both countries, with UK test R² ≈ 0.187 vs. KNN R² ≈ 0.103 (RMSE ≈ 0.451 vs. 0.474) and Japan test R² ≈ 0.138 vs. KNN R² ≈ 0.055 (RMSE ≈ 0.464 vs. 0.486). Across both countries, feature-importance rankings highlighted meaning in life, student competition, teacher support, exposure to bullying, and ICT resources, but the models explain only a modest share of variance. The paper imputes missing values via series mean and does not report applying PISA sampling/replicate weights, so results should be treated as predictive associations rather than population-representative or causal effects.
